input.question: Are human beings a particularly diverse species? It seems that we have a big range of physical characteristics and mental prowess while other species are much more homogeneous.
input.ground_truth: No. We're not all that diverse. Not much more than other animals anyways. *We* see these differences, because those are differences we use to identify individuals, and many of those differences are a result of nurture, rather than nature.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Are human beings a particularly diverse species? It seems that we have a big range of physical characteristics and mental prowess while other species are much more homogeneous.

Answer:

response.prediction:
Sure! Let’s break it down simply:

Imagine there are lots of different kinds of dogs. Some are big like Great Danes, some are tiny like Chihuahuas. Some have curly hair, some have straight hair. Some are fast, some are slow. But if you look at all the dogs together, they are still all dogs—they just look and act a little different from each other.

Now, think about people. People come in all shapes and sizes. Some are tall, some are short. Some have curly hair, some have straight hair. Some people are really good at drawing, some are really good at running, some are good at singing. Some people think in different ways, too. People can speak lots of different languages and have different kinds of families.

Even though all people are the same kind of animal (humans), we are very different from each other. More different than most other animals. That’s what we mean when we say humans are a “diverse” species. We look different and think different things, and we can do lots of different things.

So yes, human beings are a very diverse species!
